comment: The per-role resource ceilings and the quota machinery, as reviewed data. tools/check-db-limits.mjs asserts that every role×knob pair below is set by a migration with a value at or under its ceiling, and — the inverted half — that the knobs under `unavailable` are NEVER set, because on this platform they would be theatre. A limit that cannot bind is worse than no limit: a reviewer reads it as a control. SOURCE: docs/adr/20260203-resource-limits.md
bindingComment: WHAT MAKES THESE BIND, stated once so the gate's scope is honest. `ALTER ROLE x SET y` writes a pg_db_role_setting row that PostgreSQL applies when role x STARTS A SESSION — and `SET ROLE` does not start a session, so PostgreSQL alone would leave every value below inert. They bind because PostgREST reads pg_db_role_setting for the role it impersonates and applies those settings itself. Verified end to end: with anon at 2s and authenticator at 8s, a 5-second RPC through PostgREST as anon was cancelled at 2.03s (SQLSTATE 57014). The consequence is that these ceilings bound traffic arriving THROUGH PostgREST — every supabase-js call from web and mobile — and do NOT bound a direct connection (an Edge Function on a Postgres driver, a migration, psql, Supavisor session mode), which gets its own login role's settings instead.
reloadComment: AND THE RELOAD IS PART OF THE CONTROL, which is why check-db-limits.mjs requires it. This comment used to say PostgREST applied the settings 'per request'. It does not: it caches them in its SCHEMA CACHE and applies the cached copy, so a migration that changes a ceiling does not reach API traffic until that cache is rebuilt. Supabase's `pgrst_ddl_watch` event trigger issues the reload for ordinary DDL, but event triggers DO NOT FIRE for shared objects and roles are shared — so `ALTER ROLE ... SET` is exactly the statement class that never gets the automatic reload. Measured against a live stack: after `ALTER ROLE anon RESET statement_timeout` the catalog row was gone and PostgREST still reported '3s'; only after `NOTIFY pgrst, 'reload schema'` did it report the authenticator's '8s'. A fresh `supabase start` hides this completely, because PostgREST boots after migrations — the failure surfaces only on an existing project, which is the only place it costs anything.
ceilingsComment: The maximum any role may be given, in milliseconds. A migration that RAISES a value past its ceiling reds; lowering is always allowed, because tightening a limit is not a widening of anything.
unavailableComment: KNOBS THAT MUST NOT APPEAR, each because setting it here would produce a plausible number that bounds nothing. This is the inverted half of the gate and it is the half that catches the seductive mistake: both of these read as obvious hardening, both were in the original plan, and both were removed only after trying them against a real database.

unavailable.reason: Superuser-only (PGC_SUSET). `postgres` on Supabase is not a superuser, so `ALTER ROLE authenticated SET temp_file_limit` fails outright with 'permission denied to set parameter' — verified against the local stack, and the hosted project has the same role model. There is no way to set it from a migration on this platform, so a large sort still spills uncapped; that ceiling is the platform's to set, not this repo's.

The only role where a connection cap would bind is the one that LOGS IN — `authenticator` — and that is a RESERVED role: 'only superusers can modify it', verified. Setting it on anon/authenticated/service_role succeeds and is completely inert, because a connection limit applies at login and none of those three ever log in. It would put a number in pg_authid that bounds nothing, which is strictly worse than absence. Connection count is bounded by Supavisor's pool size, which is platform configuration.

quotaComment: The quota machinery's shape, asserted structurally because both wrong answers are one-word edits away and neither fails loudly. A FOR EACH ROW trigger serializes every insert behind the org's usage tuple; a RESTRICTIVE policy calling a STABLE function is hoisted to one evaluation per statement against the PRE-statement count, so a single multi-row INSERT of any size passes wholesale. Verified: 53 rows in one statement against a limit of 5 is refused by the shipped shape.

meteredTables.reason: The seeded vertical's row table, and the worked example every later metered table copies. Metering row COUNT rather than bytes because it is the number a customer understands and the only one a statement-level trigger can compute without reading the rows it is counting.
